title: Session accordion grouper: latency-aware KV-slice prioritization for streaming replies
creator: Maya Patel
description:
Problem: Streaming chat workloads show high tail latency and GPU memory churn when many short-lived conversations interleave with a few long, KV-heavy sessions. Existing batchers prioritize token coalescing but often degenerate into memory-pressure-induced KV spills, increasing end-to-end latency for interactive replies.

Proposal: Implement an "accordion grouper" batch-formation heuristic that adaptively expands and contracts virtual session groups based on live latency budgets and KV footprint. The heuristic operates continuously (no rigid scheduling epochs) and applies three core mechanisms: 1) KV-slice prioritization: when forming a candidate group, prefer sessions whose KV cache delta (estimated incremental memory if included) is below a per-GPU slice threshold; 2) Latency budget shaping: compute per-request soft deadlines from client SLOs and use a shrinking window to bias grouping toward low-deadline sessions; 3) Accordion expansion/contract: dynamically merge compatible sessions into a larger micro-batch when GPU headroom and KV-slice estimates allow, and fold them back into smaller groups when memory pressure or deadline tightness increases.

Key behaviors and safety nets:
- Prefix affinity: keep requests that share recent prefix KV entries together to reuse KV slices and reduce memory duplication.
- Soft slab caps: maintain a per-GPU soft slab allocation for KV slices with an eviction priority score (age, reuse probability, session priority).
- Backpressure escalation: if slab usage exceeds soft cap, immediately stop accordion expansion and favor minimal groups to avoid spills; expose a metric for spill-rate to SLO alarms.
- Graceful fallback: if accordion grouping fails to meet tail-latency targets, fallback to throughput-optimized packer for lower-cost non-interactive workloads.
- Simulated admission control: avoid admitting new long-KV sessions if their expected TTL would cause >10% incremental slab occupancy under median load.

Implementation plan:
1) Modeling phase (1 sprint): add a KV-slice estimator that predicts incremental GPU memory per request using token length, model layer count, and observed cache reuse. Instrument traces to collect KV-delta labels.
2) Heuristic prototype (2 sprints): implement accordion grouper in the microbatch planner with toggleable knobs (slice_threshold, expansion_rate, latency_bias). Add unit tests and synthetic workload harness.
3) Canary and benchmarks (1 sprint): run canary on dedicated cluster with mixed workloads (many short sessions + heavy long sessions). Measure 95th/99th latency, KV spill events, and token/sec.
4) Rollout and tuning (2 sprints): phased rollout with automated knob-sweeps and dashboard panels.

Success criteria:
- 99th percentile latency for interactive flows reduced by >=20% under mixed load compared to current greedy packer.
- KV spill events reduced by >=50% during peak.
- No more than 5% regression in aggregate throughput (tokens/sec) for non-interactive workloads.

Artifacts and links:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INFR/Accordion+Grouper+Design
- Benchmark harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/stream-bench/tree/accordion-experiments
- Draft PR with estimator and planner: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4876

Operational notes:
- Add metrics: kv_slice_estimated_bytes, accordion_group_size, kv_spill_rate, accordion_backpressure_count, latency_budget_missed_count.
- Dashboard: new per-cluster panel focused on accordion behavior and spill alerts.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Overly aggressive expansion may temporarily increase p99 if estimator underpredicts KV delta; mitigate with conservative initial thresholds and real-time corrective signals.
- Complexity increases in planner codepath; plan to keep feature behind feature-flag and implement comprehensive telemetry.

Next steps: wire up estimator instrumentation, implement a minimal accordion grouping prototype in the dev cluster, and run microbench harness comparisons against the current greedy microbatcher.
